title: PerfGuard: A Performance-Aware Agent for Visual Content Generation
one_liner: Plan image-generation tasks with measured tool strengths instead of vague tool descriptions, then update those preferences when real runs disagree with the plan.
lead: A visual-content agent may have many tools: image editors, layout tools, captioning tools, and style transfer tools. Most agent systems choose among them from text descriptions alone, as if each tool always works equally well. That is a bad assumption. One editor may do background replacement better because its editing controls preserve scene boundaries well, while another may handle text placement or face repair better because its outputs stay cleaner on those subtasks. PerfGuard builds an agent that keeps explicit performance records for each tool and uses those records while planning. It also updates its preferences after seeing real execution outcomes. The result is a planner that does not just ask what a tool claims to do, but asks how well that tool usually performs on the kind of subtask now in front of it.

problem.h2: Why tool descriptions are not enough
paras: An agent that builds visual content usually decomposes a request into subtasks such as generate a draft image, edit a region, add text, or improve sharpness, because each part of the request depends on a different capability. If the planner knows only a short text description of each tool, it cannot tell where one tool is strong and where another one fails.

That gap causes planning mistakes. The agent may choose a tool that is usually weak on the current subtask, or may keep using an outdated preference after the tools have changed. Visual generation is especially sensitive to this because small tool differences can change whether the final image matches the user's request.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Measure each tool on fine-grained task dimensions, plan with those scores, and keep updating the preference table when real executions reveal a better choice, because current performance matters more than a static description.

panels.title: 1. User request arrives
panels.viz_args: Make a poster, replace background, add readable text
panels.caption: A single request usually contains several different subtasks with different tool needs.

panels.title: 2. Old agent reads tool blurbs
panels.caption: A description such as "good for editing" is too coarse because it hides where the tool succeeds and where it struggles.

panels.title: 3. PerfGuard keeps score tables
panels.caption: Each tool receives measured scores on concrete subtask dimensions.

panels.title: 4. Planner chooses by fit
panels.viz_args: Subtask -> best scoring tool for that need
panels.caption: The plan aligns each subtask with the tool that has the best track record for that type of work.

panels.title: 5. Real outcomes feed back
panels.viz_args: Planned rank vs actual rank -> update preferences
panels.caption: The agent corrects its own preference table because live runs reveal when the current scores are outdated.

steps.text: Evaluate each tool on fine-grained visual subtasks, so the agent stores real performance boundaries instead of generic descriptions.
Break the user request into concrete jobs such as draft generation, region editing, text placement, or finishing touches.
Use the stored score table to predict which tool is most suitable for each job, because different jobs reward different tool strengths.

steps.b: Run the plan and inspect the outcome.
steps.text: Compare the planned ranking with what actually worked best on the executed task.
Shift the score table toward the better-performing tool, so later plans track current tool behavior instead of stale assumptions because the update records what actually worked.

paras: The paper changes tool selection from description-based matching to measured performance-based planning with online preference updates.

hidden.name: How well a tool's observed strengths match the current subtask
paras: The planner does not really need a general opinion about a tool. It needs a task-specific fit score: for this exact subtask, how likely is this tool to produce the desired result?

PerfGuard estimates that fit from multi-dimensional tool evaluations and then revises it after live runs. This matters because a tool that is excellent for one visual job can still be a poor choice for another, and the right planner must preserve those differences.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark cases where a static tool description is most likely to choose the wrong tool.

reads.html: The real question is whether a tool is good for this subtask, not whether it is good in general.
PerfGuard models task-specific fit with measured performance dimensions and updates those preferences after execution because tool behavior can drift over time.

paras: The method works because planning quality depends on the quality of the planner's beliefs about the available tools. Generic text blurbs hide real performance boundaries. Measured score tables expose those boundaries, so the planner can match each subtask to a tool that has already shown strength on similar work.

The update step matters just as much as the initial scores. A tool may improve after an update, or fail on a class of requests that the offline evaluation missed. PerfGuard corrects those beliefs after live runs, so the agent becomes more reliable over time because it learns from actual execution rather than repeating the same mistaken choice.

stages.s: Plan with the best tool-subtask matches
Updated preference table for later runs

math.words: Give each tool a score for each subtask type, then choose the tool with the highest expected fit and revise that score after observing the real result.
math.equation: tool_score(tool, subtask) = offline_fit(tool, subtask) + update(tool, subtask)
symbols: the measured score from prior evaluation on that kind of visual job
the correction added after comparing planned and actual execution outcomes
the current score used by the planner to rank tools for one subtask

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the agent must add readable text to an image and also replace the background.
Tool A has strong text-edit scores but weaker background-edit scores.
Tool B has the opposite pattern.
PerfGuard assigns Tool A to text and Tool B to background because each choice follows the measured fit table.
If Tool B unexpectedly fails on the background edit in a live run, the update term lowers its future background score.
The next plan changes because the preference table now reflects real execution feedback.

math.note: The update term is important because tool quality changes over time, and a frozen ranking table becomes stale.

bars.h2: What the result should look like

charts.title: Description-only planner
charts.note: A planner that knows only text blurbs makes many avoidable mistakes because it cannot see fine-grained performance boundaries.

charts.title: PerfGuard
charts.note: PerfGuard improves planning because measured tool scores and online updates keep the chosen tool closer to the actual need.

items.b: The evaluation table may miss important task types.
items.html: If the offline score table does not include a subtask the user later asks for, the planner still lacks useful evidence because it must extrapolate from incomplete coverage.
One bad run does not always mean the tool is bad. Preference updates must average over enough evidence because random failures should not overturn a good ranking.

items.b: The planner may overfit to one benchmark style.
items.html: If the score table is built from narrow evaluation prompts, it may rank tools well only for that prompt style and miss real user variation.

When the score table covers the main subtask types and the updates reflect real outcomes, the agent chooses better tools because planning is grounded in observed capability rather than tool marketing text.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Collect several visual-content requests that each require multiple subtasks, because composite requests expose whether the planner can match different jobs to different tools. Compare a baseline planner that chooses tools from text descriptions against a PerfGuard-style planner that uses measured subtask scores plus feedback updates. Record whether the chosen tools match an oracle ranking and whether the final image matches the request. The demo should show higher planning accuracy for the PerfGuard-style system because it reasons with real tool behavior and revises stale beliefs after execution.
demo.closing: A convincing demo shows fewer bad tool picks on composite requests because that is where performance-aware planning has to make several tool decisions instead of one.
